description: We’re a team of aerospace-minded students tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We’re building a tool that shows, for any candidate landing site near the Moon’s south pole, when the Sun is visible for solar power and when Earth is visible for direct communication, and how that changes over time.
summary:
Khonsu is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public quickly compare candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. For each of NASA’s nine Artemis candidate regions, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real local horizon at any date and time. It also shows when the site is in sunlight (power) and when Earth is visible (direct communication).

Near the south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees above the horizon, so distant ridges decide whether a site is lit. We built each site’s true skyline from NASA’s LRO laser-altimeter (LOLA) terrain data, accounting for the Moon’s curvature, and combined it with Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons. Khonsu then reports sunlit and Earth-visible percentages, time until sunset or Earthset, and the longest periods without power or communications, which drive battery sizing and mission risk.

When launch dates slip or plans change, teams need to re-evaluate sites fast. Khonsu turns complex ephemeris and terrain data into clear, comparable visuals that show why small changes in location or date matter so much.

details: A script was written to obtain position, zenith and azimuth values using a HTTP GET request to JPL Horizons API. This was then formatted and converted into a csv which was processed to find when each lunar site would be sunlit and shadowed. This was then considered in the context of the moons terrain using data from LRO LOLA. Rasterio was then used to extract information form the csv file to perform hillside shading. The forntend (UI/UX design for web application) KHONSU's interactive Planner, Orbit, and Surface views with React, TypeScript, and Three.js, integrating NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons predictions of Sun and Earth positions. Users can choose a lunar landing site and time, then explore a 72-hour forecast of sunlight and Earth (+ ground station or satellite) visibility to compare conditions for solar power and direct communications.
